summary.text: Taking \(n=7\), the conditions \(x\le y\le z\) and \(x+y+z=7\) imply \(3x\le7\), hence \(x\le2\). This contradicts the requirement \(x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}\), so the asserted restricted representation already fails at 7.

full_proof.text:
Let a valid representation of an integer \(n\) mean a triple of positive integers
\[
 x\le y\le z,\qquad x+y+z=n,
\]
for which all six integers
\[
2x-1,\quad 2y-1,\quad 2z-1,\quad 2xy-1,\quad 2xz-1,\quad 2yz-1
\]
are prime. The conjecture has two assertions: first, that every \(n>5\) has at least one valid representation; and second, the stronger “moreover” assertion that whenever \(n>6\), a valid representation can be chosen with
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]
Because the conjecture includes this second assertion, it is enough to give one integer greater than \(6\) for which the asserted special representation cannot exist.

Take
\[
n=7.
\]
Certainly \(7>6\). Suppose, for contradiction, that the “moreover” assertion holds for this value. Then there would be positive integers \(x,y,z\) satisfying
\[
x+y+z=7,
\qquad x\le y\le z,
\qquad x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\},
\]
as well as the six primality conditions.

Membership in the displayed finite set gives the five cases
\[
x=3,\quad x=4,\quad x=6,\quad x=10,\quad\text{or}\quad x=15.
\]
In particular, in every case \(x\ge 3\). Since the triple is ordered, \(x\le y\) and \(y\le z\), so both of the other entries are also at least \(x\):
\[
y\ge x\quad\text{and}\quad z\ge y\ge x.
\]
Consequently
\[
x+y+z\ge x+x+x=3x\ge 3\cdot 3=9.
\]
But the sum was required to equal \(7\). This would give \(7\ge 9\), an impossibility.

Equivalently, the individual cases make the same contradiction explicit: if \(x=3\), the ordering forces the sum to be at least \(3+3+3=9\); for \(x=4,6,10,15\), it forces the sum to be at least \(12,18,30,45\), respectively. Thus none of the five allowed values of \(x\) can occur in an ordered positive triple summing to \(7\).

The primality requirements do not need to be considered, because no triple satisfies even the preceding elementary size, ordering, and sum requirements. Hence \(n=7\) has no valid representation whose least entry \(x\) belongs to \(\{3,4,6,10,15\}\). This directly falsifies the conjecture’s claim that every integer \(n>6\) has such a representation. Since that claim is one conjunct of the stated conjecture, the entire conjecture is false.
